fields.claim_quote: Since $x_{i}$ is the number of members of $j$ that satisfy $i<j$ and are before $i$ in a list based on $\text{MF}$ before the operation $s_{l}$ follows $\Phi\left(D_{l-1}\right)=x_{l}$.
fields.explanation: The source defines Phi as the number of all inverted unordered pairs between the two lists, whereas x_i counts only inversions involving the accessed item. Inversions between other items contribute to Phi but not x_i. In the original state MF=[1,0,2], A=[0,1,2], accessing item 2 has Phi=1 and x_2=0. The state is reachable from the source empty initial lists: insert 2, then 1, then 0 at the front in both lists, and then access 1, with A making no exchange and MF moving 1 to the front. This produces exactly the original witness lists. The corrected identity concerns the change in potential: moving item i to the front removes x_i inversions and creates k-1-x_i inversions, giving Phi_after-Phi_before=k-1-2*x_i when A makes no exchanges. On the witness this change is 3-1=2. This refutes the intermediate absolute-potential identity, not the final 2-competitiveness theorem.
fields.flaw: Reading the printed x_l as the previously defined x_i for the accessed item, the asserted absolute identity Phi(D_(l-1))=x_i omits inversions between other items. The selected witness has Phi=1 and x_i=0. This diagnosis preserves the source's x_l quotation and makes the interpretive substitution explicit.
fields.problem: Prove: Self-organizing list that uses Move-to-Front is 2-Competitive
fields.source_context:
0018 | 
0019 | The papier is great but I feel it skips a lot of steps in their solution. I'm trying to re-write the proof but without skipping any steps. Here is what I did:
0020 | 
0021 | > By using the potential method, the potential function $\Phi$ will be defined as the number of inversions $(i,j)$ whose order of appearance in the list based on algorithm $\text{MF}$ is different from the order of their appearance in list based on algorithm $A$. That is, the potential function will count the pairings $(i,j)$ in which $i$ appears before $j$ in an $A$-based list and after $j$ in a $\text{MF}$-based list or $i$ appears before $j$ in a $\text{MF}$-based list and after $j$ in an $A$-based list. The potential function treats pairs in an unordered manner, meaning that the pair $(i,j)$ is the same as the pair $(j,i)$.
0022 | >
0023 | > We start from two empty lists, so at the beginning of the series of operations, the potential is $\Phi\left(D_{0}\right)=0$. Also, for all $l$ the potential is positive, since $\Phi\left(D_{l}\right)\geq\Phi\left(D_{0}\right)=0$ holds.
0024 | >
0025 | > We will analyze the amortized time of the $\text{MF}$ algorithm for each operation $s_{l}$ as a function of the cost of the operation in algorithm $A$. **We will first discuss the search operation** of element $i$. Without limiting generality, let's assume that the $A$-based list consists of the elements $1,2,3,\ldots,i,i+1,\ldots$ (this assumption is possible because it can be obtained by changing the names of the elements in lists based on $A$ and $\text{MF}$).
0026 | >
0027 | > Let $x_{i}$ be the number of members $j$ that hold $i<j$ and are before $i$ in the list based on $\text{MF}$ (before the operation $s_{l}$). Since we assume an order in which the $j$-th member in the list based on $A$ is $j$, we will get that $x_{i}$ is the number of members $j$ that appear after $i$ in the based list $A$ and before $i$ in the based list $\text{MF}$. In addition, let $k$ be the index of member $i$ in the based list $\text{MF}$. Therefore, out of $k-1$ members preceding member $i$ in the list based on $\text{MF}$, $x_{i}$ of which do not precede $i$ in the based list $A$ and exactly $k-1-x_{i}$ also precede $i$ in the based list $A$.
0028 | >
0029 | > According to the $\text{MF}$ algorithm, it follows that after performing the $s_{l}$ operation, element $i$ is moved to the top of the $\text{MF}$-based list. We will separate cases according to the types of pairs $(i,j)$:
0030 | > - Assume that before the move, $j$ appeared before $i$ in both lists. Therefore, after the move, $j$ will appear after $i$ in a list based on $\text{MF}$ and before $i$ in a list based on $A$. Since $x_{i}$ is the number of members of $j$ that satisfy $i<j$ and are before $i$ in a list based on $\text{MF}$ before the operation $s_{l}$ follows $\Phi\left(D_{l-1}\right)=x_{l}$. In this case, after performing the $s_{l}$ operation, $i$ is moved to the top of the $\text{MF}$ based list. Therefore, $k-1-x_{i}$ elements that appeared before $i$ in both lists, now appear after $i$ in the $\text{MF}$ based list and before $i$ in the $A$ based list. Also, $x_{i}$ elements that appeared before $i$ in the $\text{MF}$ and after $i$ in the based list $A$, now appear after $i$ in both lists. Thus $\Phi\left(D_{l}\right)=k-1-x_{i}+y$ where $y$ is the contribution of the paid operations and the free operations. We will divide into sub-cases:
0031 | >    - Assume that $X_{A}(l)=0$ and $F_{A}(l)=0$. $X_{A}(l)=0$ holds and therefore no paid operation was performed. Also, $F_{A}(l)=0$ holds and therefore no free operation was performed. In this case, we get $y=0$, i.e. $\Phi\left(D_{l}\right)=k-1-x_{i}$. It follows that the change in potential is:
0032 | $$
0033 | \Delta\Phi=\Phi\left(D_{l}\right)-\Phi\left(D_{l-1}\right)=\left(k-1-x_{i}\right)-x_{ i}=k-1-2x_{i}
0034 | $$
0035 | The actual cost of this operation is $c_{l}=k$ and therefore we get:
0036 | $$
0037 | \hat{c}_{l}=c_{l}+\Phi\left(D_{l}\right)-\Phi\left(D_{l-1}\right)=c_{l}+\Delta \Phi=k+\left(k-1-2x_{i}\right)=2\left(k-x_{i}\right)-1
0038 | $$
0039 | Since there are $k-1$ elements prior to $i$ in a list based on $\text{MF}$ and only the elements $\{1,2,\ldots,i-1\}$ do not contribute to $x_{i}$ (the rest of the elements necessarily contribute to $x_{i}$), it follows that $x_{i}\geq k-i$ holds. From this it follows that $k-x_{i}\leq i$ holds and therefore we get:
0040 | $$
0041 | \hat{c}_{l}=2\left(k-x_{i}\right)-1\leq2i-1=2i+0-0-1
0042 | $$
fields.witness: Interpret the source’s printed x_l as x_i for the accessed item, as defined immediately before the quote; retain x_l verbatim in the source quote. Start from empty lists and insert2,1,0 at the front in both algorithms, obtaining[0,1,2]. Now let the comparator make no exchanges. Access1 under MTF, giving[1,0,2], then consider access to item2. Before that access, the persistent inversion{0,1} gives Phi=1, whereas x_2=0. After moving2 to the front, Phi=3. Thus the intended absolute identity Phi=x_i fails; the change in potential is3-1=2, as the usual local-pair calculation gives.
